$about: 2026-08-06: the three severe findings logged on 2026-08-04 that are missing vocabulary rather than broken scripts (SEC-02, LOOP-03, DEC-08), each re-run against the current tree before anything was written. They had not aged the same way. Two still reproduce and are fixed here; the third was closed the same evening it was logged, by a pull request whose body predated the commit that closed it, and is proved closed rather than re-fixed. The observations keep the 2026-08-04 round's target label so they supersede those findings on the punch list; each evidence field states which tree the run was executed against and what was NOT verified.

observations.evidence: Reproduced first, by the case's own two-part procedure against the current tree. (1) `grep -n -i -E 'embargo|confidential|not yet public|private (repo|mirror|fork)|disclos' standard/SPEC.md` exited 1 with no output - not one of R3, R11 or R15 carried an embargo or confidentiality clause, and neither did any other rule. (2) The manifest exceptions schema: `EXCEPTION_KINDS = ["file", "section", "content", "key"]` in `standard/scripts/self-verify.mjs`, and an unknown kind is a FAIL naming the valid ones, so an `embargo` kind could not have been recorded even informally. `grep -rn -i -E 'embargo|confidential' docs/method/ standard/` returned nothing at all - across the whole tree the words appeared only inside the validation suite's own data (this case, its rendered rows, and one target's description of somebody else's SECURITY.md). Fixed by naming the case rather than by weakening R3. R3 gains a clause: work whose *publication* is itself the harm may be held in a private mirror of the repo (the platform's private advisory fork named as the paved road) and MUST rejoin the mainline when the embargo lifts; every rule binds inside that mirror, so the spec, the coupled change (R11), the backlog intent (R15) and the changelog entry are written while the work happens rather than reconstructed at disclosure. That is why only one rule moved - once 'the repo' may temporarily be private, R11 and R15 are satisfied inside it and need no exception, which is the shape the case's `then` asked for and one hole instead of three. The clause is bounded at the start (a lifting condition and an owner, named the moment the embargo begins; one with no stated end is called out as the R3 violation it already was) and names its near misses out loud ('not written up yet', 'it is in the chat', work someone would rather not publish are not embargoes; a repo that is already private needs none of it). Recorded as ADR-033 with both rejected options: an 'unless confidential' clause on each of the three rules, and a new `embargo` kind in the manifest's `exceptions` - rejected on what `exceptions` is, a repo's standing structural deviation read at drift time that deliberately lowers the adoption percentage, which would have penalised the correct behaviour and left a permanent artifact of a temporary condition. `docs/method/security-baseline.md` gains an `Embargoed work` axis, so the security decision R19 already requires answers where embargoed work lives and who lifts it. What is NOT claimed: nothing mechanical checks that an embargo was legitimate or that it lifted - the lifting condition and its owner are prose, and ADR-033's Confirmation section says so rather than implying a guard exists. No embargoed change has been driven through the private-mirror path end to end; what is verified is that the vocabulary now exists and that the same grep now finds it.

Does not reproduce against the current tree, and was already closed before this round opened - the finding and its fix landed the same evening, and the round never re-ran. The case's own procedure, `grep -rn -i revisit` across every `standard/.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md` and every `scripts/*.mjs`, returned on 2026-08-04 two writers (`adr-write`, `bdr-write`) and zero readers. It now returns those two writers plus six hits in `discovery-digest`, whose step 4 pulls each record's `Revisit when` across `docs/decision-records/` and checks incoming material against it; the scripts still return zero, which is by design - the step is a grep an agent runs, not a guard. Closed by commit `dbdbc18` in PR #14, whose title names the defect ('the record layer wrote but nobody read it back') and whose body predates that commit, which is why the round that logged it did not see it. Verified mechanically rather than by reading the step, because the original finding was that the mechanism only fired on an agent's own memory: pulling every `## Revisit when` block across the fixture's five records (`awk '/^## Revisit when/{flag=1;next}/^## /{flag=0}flag'`) and matching a new, unseen entry ('she has stopped reading the swap requests properly - approval fatigue, she just taps yes now') against them produced `HIT docs/decision-records/bdr/BDR-001-manager-is-the-primary-persona.md <- 'approval'` and `<- 'fatigue'` - the record whose trigger actually fired - with no agent memory in the loop, plus one noise hit on ADR-001 for the word 'volume', which is the expected cost of a grep and is why step 4 makes a hit a row for a human rather than an automatic supersession. Not re-fixed here. What is NOT claimed: this closes a tripwire on material entering through a discovery handover, which is what the case specifies. A signal true in the world and never filed here still reaches nothing, and the step says so in its own text; `docs/method/dev-work.md`, which introduced the revisit-when field and named nothing that reads it back, now points at the skill that does and states the same limit.

Still reproduces, and is a different hole from the retirement work that landed since. Run literally against the fixture: `specs/shift-swap-request/spec.md` carries `**Status:** in-refinement`, so step 1's retired-capability stop does not fire, and the change under analysis (auto-approval for low-risk swaps) is explicitly forbidden by Accepted `BDR-001-manager-is-the-primary-persona.md`, whose `What this rules out` reads 'Auto-approval as the default for any swap, for now.' Step 3's second bullet said '**ADRs** - does the change need a new/superseding decision, or contradict an Accepted ADR?', which sends the agent to `docs/decision-records/adr/` - `ls` gives `ADR-001-postgres-as-the-datastore.md`, a README and the template, and `grep -rli auto-approv docs/decision-records/adr/` returns nothing. The documented output line was 'ADR impact: none / new / supersede'. `grep -rin auto-approv docs/decision-records/bdr/` finds the answer on line 46 of BDR-001, in the directory the step never names. Fixed by making the bullet read both streams, name the BDR's `What this rules out` as the only section that carries a capability's non-goals, and say why the ADR-only reading answers a different question: what a change may not do is usually a business constraint - a licence boundary, a vendor or customer contract, a regulatory limit, a persona call. The output line now reports decision-record impact across ADR and BDR, with `contradicts` as its own outcome. `specs/spec-engine/spec.md` gains the requirement and the acceptance criterion, so the coupling guard holds the skill and its spec together; `spec-guard --base main --block` and `--audit --block` both pass. What is NOT claimed: this is a change to the analysis step's instructions, not a mechanical check - nothing fails a pull request that contradicts an Accepted BDR. The shipped pull-request template's own section is still headed 'ADR impact' with four ADR-only checkboxes; that is a second, human-facing surface with the same blind spot, deliberately left out of this change's scope and named here rather than fixed silently.
